title: An idempotent queue consumer
prompt:
When a student finishes a book, the app publishes a book.completed message, and a worker awards 10 XP. The queue delivers at least once: after a timeout or a worker crash the same message can arrive again, possibly at a second worker. Without protection, students get 20 or 30 XP. Wrap the handler so its effect happens once per idempotency key.

API: new IdempotentConsumer(handler, store = new Map()). The store can be shared between consumer instances (think: a Redis or a database table both workers can see).

async handle(msg) where msg = { id, idempotencyKey?, body }. The dedupe key is msg.idempotencyKey if present, otherwise msg.id. Returns:

  • { status: 'processed', result } the first time, after await handler(msg) succeeds.
  • { status: 'duplicate', result } for a key already processed, returning the stored result without calling the handler.
  • { status: 'in_progress' } if another delivery with the same key is being handled right now (don't run the handler twice in parallel).
  • If the handler throws, rethrow the error and forget the key so a redelivery can try again.

tests.name: processes a new message and returns the handler result
a redelivered message is not applied twice
different messages are each processed
dedupes on idempotencyKey when present, not on message id
a failed attempt can be retried by redelivery
concurrent duplicate delivery runs the handler once
two workers sharing a store process a message once

hints: Compute the key first: const key = msg.idempotencyKey ?? msg.id. Then look it up in this.store before calling the handler.
To stop a parallel duplicate, write { state: 'in_progress' } to the store before you await the handler. Anything that runs during the await will see that marker.
Wrap the handler call in try/catch: on success store { state: 'done', result }; on failure this.store.delete(key) and rethrow.
explain:
Queues like SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka (by default) give you at-least-once delivery, so "exactly once" is something the consumer builds: at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively once. In production the store is a database table with a unique constraint on the key (ideally written in the same transaction as the XP update, so the two can never disagree), or a Redis SET key NX EX 86400. The in-progress marker needs a timeout too, or a worker that crashes mid-handler would block the key forever.

In an interview: "Delivery is at-least-once, so every consumer is idempotent. I dedupe on a business key like complete:student:book, recorded in the same transaction as the side effect, and I return the stored result for duplicates."
